questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to automatically update a related parent Account rating when an Opportunity is closed won.
questions.question: Which approach should the App Builder recommend FIRST, following the 'clicks-not-code' best practice?

options.text: Write an Apex trigger on Opportunity to update the Account rating.
Create a Record-Triggered Flow on Opportunity.
Build a Lightning Web Component that runs on the Opportunity record page.
Use a Visualforce page with a controller extension.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Salesforce best practice is to solve problems declaratively first. A Record-Triggered Flow on Opportunity can update the parent Account without code. A is wrong because Apex should only be used when declarative tools cannot meet the requirement (Process Builder and Workflow Rules are being retired; Flow is the recommended declarative automation). C is wrong because LWCs are for UI, not backend automation. D is wrong because Visualforce is legacy UI technology and not intended for backend automation.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Flow Builder / Trailhead: Automate Your Business Processes

questions.scenario: Universal Containers must call an external REST service to retrieve real-time inventory data and display the result on a custom Lightning page in less than 2 seconds.
questions.question: Which solution is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a Record-Triggered Flow with an HTTP callout action.
Use an External Service imported through the setup UI, invoked declaratively from Flow.
Build a Lightning Web Component backed by an Apex controller that performs the callout.
Add a Web Tab that opens the external system directly.

questions.explanation: C is correct: Real-time UI display with sub-second responsiveness and complex data handling is best handled by an LWC with an Apex controller that performs the callout. A is wrong because record-triggered flows are not the right pattern to render results in the UI on demand. B (External Service + Flow) is a valid low-code option but is generally slower and better suited for automation than for rendering data on a page in real time. D is wrong because a Web Tab embeds an external app but does not display inventory data inline on the Salesforce record page.
questions.reference: Salesforce Developer Guide: Apex Callouts / LWC Developer Guide

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty is deciding when to use declarative tools vs Apex code.
questions.question: Which two scenarios REQUIRE a programmatic solution (Apex or LWC)? (Choose 2)

options.text: Complex sharing logic that changes based on multiple record fields at runtime.
Sending an email alert when a Case is escalated.
Running batch processing on more than 250,000 records nightly with custom transaction control.
Assigning a task to the Opportunity owner when a stage changes.

questions.explanation: A and C are correct. A: Custom Apex Managed Sharing is required when sharing depends on runtime record data that OWD, sharing rules, and manual sharing cannot express. C: Batch Apex is the correct tool for large-volume, transactional processing with fine-grained governor-limit control. B is wrong because Email Alerts driven by Flow are fully declarative. D is wrong because Record-Triggered Flow can create tasks declaratively.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Apex Managed Sharing / Batch Apex

questions.scenario: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) wants a screen that guides a rep through multi-step lead qualification with branching logic and record creation.
questions.question: Which declarative option is most appropriate?

options.text: A Visualforce page with a controller.
A Screen Flow launched from a Lightning action.
A Lightning Web Component with custom JavaScript state machine.
A Quick Action with a predefined field layout.

questions.explanation: B is correct: A Screen Flow is the declarative tool built exactly for multi-step, branching user interactions with data creation. A is wrong because Visualforce is legacy and unnecessary here. C is wrong because it requires code when a declarative option exists. D is wrong because Quick Actions provide a single-page form, not multi-step branching wizards.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar needs to enforce a complex validation across three parent-child object relationships that Flow and Validation Rules cannot easily express.
questions.question: What should the App Builder recommend?

options.text: Create nested formula fields to bring parent values to the child record and use a Validation Rule.
Build a Validation Rule on each object, one at a time.
Use an Apex trigger with helper class to enforce cross-object logic.
Use Workflow Rules with multiple field updates.

questions.explanation: C is correct: When cross-object logic exceeds the capability of formulas and validation rules (for example, iterating child collections or applying complex conditions across grandparent records), an Apex trigger is the appropriate programmatic solution. A can work for some scenarios but is limited (formulas cannot iterate collections). B fails because independent validation rules cannot express the cross-object condition. D is wrong because Workflow Rules are retired and cannot enforce validation.
questions.reference: Salesforce Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.scenario: An App Builder at Cloud Kicks needs to display a highly interactive custom chart on a record page that uses a third-party JavaScript charting library.
questions.question: Which solution is best?

options.text: Add a standard Report chart component to the record page.
Use the standard Dashboard component on the record page.
Build a Lightning Web Component that renders the third-party chart.
Use a Screen Flow with display text.

questions.explanation: C is correct: Highly interactive UI using an external JS library requires an LWC. A and B are standard components and cannot host arbitrary third-party JS libraries. D is a screen flow, which is not designed for record-page interactive charts.
questions.reference: LWC Developer Guide: Third-Party JavaScript Libraries

questions.scenario: A business analyst needs to send an outbound HTTP message when an Opportunity moves to Closed Won, and wants to avoid code.
questions.question: Which declarative option should the App Builder choose in Summer '26?

options.text: Workflow Rule Outbound Message.
Process Builder HTTP callout.
Flow with an HTTP Callout action (External Service or invocable action).
Apex trigger with @future callout.

questions.explanation: C is correct: In Summer '26, Flow supports HTTP Callout actions and External Services, allowing declarative outbound calls. A is technically still available but Workflow Rules are being retired and no longer the recommended path. B is wrong because Process Builder is retired. D is a code solution and unnecessary when Flow can do it.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Flow HTTP Callout / External Services

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to extend their org with pre-built Agentforce agents, topics, and actions from a Salesforce partner.
questions.question: Which marketplace should they use?

options.text: AppExchange.
AgentExchange.
Trailhead Exchange.
Setup Home.

questions.explanation: B is correct: AgentExchange is the Salesforce marketplace dedicated to Agentforce agents, actions, topics, and prompt templates from partners. A is wrong because AppExchange hosts managed packages and general Salesforce solutions but is not the dedicated marketplace for agents. C is not a real product name. D is where you configure settings but not a marketplace.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers is browsing AgentExchange to enrich their Agentforce Service Agent.
questions.question: Which two types of components can they install from AgentExchange? (Choose 2)

options.text: Pre-built Agent Actions (invocable actions, prompt templates).
Topics for Agentforce agents packaged by partners.
Sandbox refresh templates.
Standard Salesforce license SKUs.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: AgentExchange distributes agent actions and topics (plus complete agents) from Salesforce and partners. C is wrong because sandbox templates are not distributed through AgentExchange. D is wrong because licenses are procured through Salesforce sales channels, not AgentExchange.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty wants to install a partner-built Agentforce package that includes a topic 'Property Recommendations' and three related actions.
questions.question: What best describes the install experience?

options.text: Users manually rebuild the topic and actions inside their org after downloading a spec.
The partner content is delivered as a managed package containing the topic and actions, installed through the AgentExchange listing.
AgentExchange listings can only be reviewed; they cannot be installed.
Only Salesforce Support can install AgentExchange content into an org.

questions.explanation: B is correct: AgentExchange listings are delivered as managed packages or unmanaged bundles that install topics, actions, and prompt templates directly into the org. A is wrong because rebuilding manually defeats the purpose of a marketplace. C is wrong because listings are installable. D is wrong because installation is self-service by an admin with the appropriate permissions.

questions.scenario: Northern Trail Outfitters is evaluating an AgentExchange listing.
questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about AgentExchange vs AppExchange?

options.text: AgentExchange and AppExchange are the same marketplace with two names.
AgentExchange specifically curates Agentforce assets (agents, actions, topics, prompt templates), while AppExchange covers a broader catalog including apps, components, and consulting.
AppExchange only sells hardware, while AgentExchange sells software.
AgentExchange requires a Data Cloud license to browse.

questions.explanation: B is correct: AgentExchange is the specialized marketplace for Agentforce assets; AppExchange is broader. A is wrong because they are distinct catalogs. C is wrong because AppExchange never sold hardware. D is wrong because browsing does not require Data Cloud licensing.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks installed an AgentExchange package that adds a new topic 'Order Returns' with three actions to their Agentforce Service Agent. Users report the actions are not invoked by the agent.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The topic classifications and action descriptions haven't been reviewed and assigned to the agent, so the planner cannot route utterances to them.
AgentExchange packages cannot be used by Agentforce Service Agent.
The org needs a fresh Sandbox refresh before AgentExchange content is usable.
The agent must be manually retrained via an Einstein Studio ML flow.

questions.explanation: A is correct: After installing partner topics and actions, an admin must attach them to the target agent and verify classifications/descriptions so the planner can select them. B is false. C is not a requirement. D confuses model retraining with agent configuration — Agentforce planners use LLM reasoning and metadata, not custom ML retraining.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Configure Agentforce Topics and Actions

questions.scenario: A partner published an AgentExchange listing that includes prompt templates.
questions.question: Where in the target org do the prompt templates land after install?

options.text: In the Files tab as attachments.
In Prompt Builder (Prompt Template Manager).
In Setup > Email Templates.
In the Report Builder.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Prompt templates delivered by AgentExchange installs appear in Prompt Builder, where admins can review and activate them. A is wrong because Files hold documents, not prompt metadata. C is wrong because Email Templates are for email content. D is wrong because Report Builder is for reports.

questions.scenario: An admin is comparing two AgentExchange listings.
questions.question: Which metadata should the admin review to understand what will be added to the org?

options.text: The Package Contents (agents, topics, actions, prompt templates, Flows, Apex) documented on the listing.
The developer's LinkedIn profile.
The regional data residency clauses only.
The Chatter feed of the partner.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Listings publish a components manifest so admins can understand what will be installed. B, C, D are not the primary artifacts used to evaluate what the package installs.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants to trial an AgentExchange package before installing it in production.
questions.question: What is the recommended path?

options.text: Install directly into production because managed packages can always be uninstalled.
Install into a sandbox or Developer Edition org to evaluate before production install.
Rebuild the package manually in production to test.
Ask Salesforce Support to test on behalf of the customer.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Sandboxes (or DE orgs) are the standard trial environment. A is risky and not a best practice. C misses the point of a marketplace. D is not how Salesforce Support engages.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: AgentExchange Trial Best Practices

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to restrict who can see Account records so only the owner and their manager can view them by default.
questions.question: Which setting should the App Builder configure?

options.text: Set Account OWD to Private and rely on the role hierarchy.
Create a Sharing Rule granting Read to All Internal Users.
Remove Account access from every profile.
Use Field-Level Security to hide the Account Name.

questions.explanation: A is correct: OWD Private restricts access to the owner; role hierarchy grants access up the chain (owner + managers). B would open the object to everyone, the opposite of the requirement. C would break access entirely, including for owners. D restricts one field, not the record.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty wants to EXTEND access to records beyond the OWD baseline.
questions.question: Which two mechanisms EXTEND record access? (Choose 2)

options.text: Sharing Rules.
Restriction Rules.
Manual Sharing.
Field-Level Security.

questions.explanation: A and C EXTEND access beyond the OWD baseline. B (Restriction Rules) RESTRICTS access — it filters records users can see even if they otherwise have access. D controls FIELD access, not record access.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Sharing Rules / Manual Sharing

questions.scenario: Universal Containers has OWD Public Read/Write on Case, but the Compliance team should only be able to view Cases where Type = 'Regulatory'.
questions.question: Which feature should be used?

options.text: Sharing Rule.
Restriction Rule.
Field-Level Security.
Permission Set.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Restriction Rules filter which records a specified user group can see, even when OWD would otherwise grant access. A is wrong because Sharing Rules extend access, not restrict. C hides fields, not records. D grants permissions but does not filter which records are visible.

questions.scenario: NTO wants users on the Sales team to have record access default to their own territory but be able to temporarily see records in other territories only within the current fiscal quarter.
questions.question: Which feature should the App Builder use?

options.text: Scoping Rules.
Restriction Rules.
Territory Management OWD.
Manual Sharing.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Scoping Rules define a default subset of records users see, without changing what they can access. Users can override the scope from the UI to see other records they have access to. B restricts and cannot be temporarily overridden by the user. C is not a specific OWD setting. D is manual and not automated by territory logic.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks needs a subset of users to have edit access to the Salary field on Employee, while everyone else should not see it.
questions.question: Which combination should the App Builder configure?

options.text: Set OWD on Employee to Private.
Configure Field-Level Security on the Salary field and grant it via a Permission Set assigned to the authorized users.
Encrypt the Salary field with Shield Platform Encryption for everyone.
Add a Validation Rule that prevents edits by unauthorized profiles.

questions.explanation: B is correct: FLS controls who can read/edit a specific field; using a Permission Set enforces the exception cleanly. A controls record access, not field access. C encrypts data at rest but does not hide the field from users with FLS access. D can block edits but doesn't hide the field from view.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar wants a group of specialists to be granted access to records dynamically based on data in the record (for example, based on a custom field 'Region__c' at runtime).
questions.question: Which is the most appropriate solution when standard sharing tools cannot express the criteria?

options.text: Owner-based Sharing Rule.
Criteria-based Sharing Rule.
Apex Managed Sharing.
Role hierarchy grant.

questions.explanation: C is correct: When sharing must be applied to a specific record set determined at runtime by complex logic beyond criteria-based rules, Apex Managed Sharing is the appropriate solution. A shares by owner and doesn't match. B works only when a static criteria can express the condition. D grants access up the hierarchy, not laterally by field value.
questions.reference: Salesforce Developer Guide: Apex Managed Sharing

questions.scenario: An admin needs to grant a single user extra permissions temporarily without changing their profile.
questions.question: What is the recommended tool in Summer '26?

options.text: Clone the profile and reassign the user.
Use a Permission Set (or Permission Set Group) with expiration date.
Add the user to the System Administrator profile temporarily.
Manually edit the user's field-level security everywhere.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Permission Sets and Permission Set Groups can be assigned with an expiration date, aligning with Salesforce's direction to move permissions out of profiles. A is heavier and not aligned with the direction of Salesforce. C is a security anti-pattern. D is impractical and error-prone.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Permission Set Assignments with Expiration

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks has OWD on Opportunity set to Private. The VP of Sales must see all Opportunities owned by anyone in the Sales branch of the hierarchy.
questions.question: Which mechanism grants that access automatically?

options.text: Manual Sharing on each Opportunity.
The Role Hierarchy.
A Public Group named 'Sales Leaders'.
A Restriction Rule targeting the VP.

questions.explanation: B is correct: The role hierarchy automatically grants users access to records owned by users lower in the hierarchy (assuming 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' is enabled for that object). A doesn't scale. C alone doesn't grant record access. D restricts, not extends.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants Account Team members to share access to an Account, its Opportunities, and Cases automatically when they are added to the team.
questions.question: Which feature should the App Builder recommend?

options.text: Account Teams (with team member access settings).
A Sharing Rule based on public groups.
Manual Sharing on each related record.
Role hierarchy alone.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Account Teams provide a standard model to grant team members access to the Account and its child records with granular settings per role. B is possible but heavier and less dynamic per team member. C doesn't scale. D grants access vertically, not horizontally by team.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty must grant a group of external Experience Cloud users access to specific Property__c records that match their Region__c value.
questions.question: Which TWO sharing techniques could accomplish this? (Choose 2)

options.text: Criteria-based Sharing Rule targeting the appropriate Experience Cloud user group by Region__c.
Apex Managed Sharing invoked from an Apex trigger.
Manual sharing added by each internal owner on every record.
OWD set to Public Read/Write for the Property__c object.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: Criteria-based Sharing Rules and Apex Managed Sharing can both grant external users access to a filtered set of records. C is not scalable and error-prone. D exposes all Property records to everyone, breaking the requirement.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Sharing with Experience Cloud Users

questions.scenario: An admin wants a specific user to be able to delegate certain administrative tasks (like resetting passwords and managing users in a role) without granting full System Admin.
questions.question: Which Salesforce feature should be used?

options.text: Delegated Administration.
Super User access.
Apex Managed Sharing.
Sharing Rule.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Delegated Administration Groups allow scoped admin capabilities without granting full System Admin. B refers to a Partner community feature and doesn't grant admin capabilities generally. C and D are sharing mechanisms, not admin delegation.

questions.scenario: NTO's partner users need access to the Cases owned by other partner users at the same partner account (elevated within their account).
questions.question: Which sharing capability applies?

options.text: Super User Access (Partner).
Role Hierarchy across partners.
Apex Managed Sharing to All Partners.
Public Group with Read/Write across the org.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Partner Super User Access grants a partner user access to data owned by other users in their same partner account, without exposing data across accounts. B doesn't apply — partners don't share a role hierarchy that way. C is heavy and unnecessary for a standard capability. D would over-share.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Partner Super User Access

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks has Account OWD Private. When an Account owner has access to an Account, the owner automatically gains access to the child Opportunities and Cases as well.
questions.question: What is this behavior called?

options.text: Implicit Sharing (parent-to-child).
Apex Managed Sharing.
Cascade Sharing Rule.
Owner-based Sharing Rule.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Implicit sharing gives Account owners access to child Opportunity, Case, and Contact records, and gives child-record users the ability to view the parent Account. B, C, D are unrelated: Apex Managed Sharing is code-driven, there is no 'Cascade Sharing Rule', and Owner-based Sharing Rules don't describe this behavior.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar has OWD on Opportunity Private with role hierarchy enabled. The Marketing team (a public group across roles) needs Read-Only access to all Opportunities in Stage 'Prospecting' or 'Qualification'.
questions.question: What is the best solution?

options.text: Change OWD to Public Read Only.
Create a Criteria-Based Sharing Rule granting Read Only to the Marketing public group where Stage IN ('Prospecting','Qualification').
Add each marketer to the role hierarchy above every Opportunity owner.
Give every marketer Modify All Data.

questions.explanation: B is correct: A criteria-based sharing rule perfectly targets a subset of records to a specific group. A over-shares. C is not feasible or maintainable. D is a massive over-permission.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers is designing sharing. They want the simplest baseline for a custom object 'Warranty_Claim__c' that most users can see and edit, with a few sensitive claims restricted.
questions.question: What is the recommended pattern?

options.text: OWD Public Read/Write, with Restriction Rules for the sensitive claim subset.
OWD Private, and grant every user access with manual sharing per record.
OWD Public Read Only with FLS blocking edits.
Delete OWD to remove all defaults.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Public Read/Write plus a Restriction Rule for the sensitive subset matches the requirement with the least overhead. B is unscalable. C prevents edits for everyone, not the goal. D is not a valid option — OWD cannot be deleted.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: OWD and Restriction Rules

questions.scenario: An admin at Cloud Kicks wants a report that groups Opportunities by Stage and shows subtotals for the Amount field.
questions.question: Which report format should they use?

options.text: Tabular.
Summary.
Matrix.
Joined.

questions.explanation: B is correct: A Summary report groups rows by one dimension and supports subtotals. A (Tabular) is a flat list with no groupings and no subtotals. C (Matrix) groups by both rows and columns — more than needed here. D (Joined) is for combining multiple report blocks.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers needs a report showing Opportunities by Stage (rows) and Fiscal Quarter (columns).
questions.question: Which report format is most appropriate?

options.text: Tabular.
Summary.
Matrix.
Joined.

questions.explanation: C is correct: Matrix reports group by rows AND columns. A can't group. B groups by one dimension. D combines blocks but is not the standard way to cross-tab two dimensions.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty wants a single report that shows Opportunities alongside related Cases for the same Account.
questions.question: Which report format should be used?

options.text: Tabular.
Summary.
Matrix.
Joined.

questions.explanation: D is correct: Joined reports combine multiple report blocks from different report types with a shared field. A, B, C are single-block formats.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to categorize Opportunities on the fly in a report by grouping Amount into 'Small (<10K)', 'Medium (10-100K)', 'Large (>100K)' without creating a new field on the object.
questions.question: Which report feature should be used?

options.text: Custom Formula Field.
Bucket Field.
Cross Filter.
Roll-Up Summary.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Bucket Fields categorize values in-report without adding an object field. A adds an object field, not required. C filters records across related objects. D aggregates child values on a parent record.

questions.scenario: NTO needs a report showing Accounts that have no Opportunities in the last 90 days.
questions.question: Which report feature helps most?

options.text: Cross Filter with 'without' condition on Opportunities.
Bucket Field.
Historical Trend Report.
Roll-Up Summary.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Cross filters let you include or exclude records based on the presence/absence of related records with specific criteria. B categorizes values. C compares data snapshots over time. D is an object aggregation feature.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar wants to compare current Opportunity Amounts against values from 30 and 60 days ago.
questions.question: Which reporting capability supports this?

options.text: Historical Trend Reporting.
Bucket Field.
Cross Filter.
Joined Report Block.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Historical Trend Reporting captures snapshots of specific fields (up to 8 fields on select objects) so users can compare values over time. B, C, D don't provide time-based snapshots.

questions.scenario: An admin at Universal Containers wants each Sales Manager to see the SAME dashboard, but with data filtered to their own team.
questions.question: Which capability best fits?

options.text: Dynamic Dashboards with 'View As' running user or dashboard filters.
A separate static dashboard per manager.
Historical Trend Reporting.
Report subscription.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Dynamic Dashboards run in the context of the logged-in user (or a selected user) so each manager sees their own team's data without maintaining duplicate dashboards. B is not scalable. C compares data over time, not per user. D delivers a fixed dashboard result on schedule.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks reports need to include fields from multiple related objects (Account, Contact, Custom_Object__c) that the standard report types don't expose together.
questions.question: What should the App Builder do?

options.text: Create a Custom Report Type joining the required objects.
Modify the standard Contact & Account report type.
Use a Bucket Field to bring the related fields in.
Use a Cross Filter to add columns.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Custom Report Types define which objects/relationships and fields are available for reports. B is not possible — standard report types cannot be modified. C only categorizes values on the record — it doesn't add related object fields. D filters records but does not add columns.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty wants users to receive an emailed report on a schedule and receive notifications when values cross a threshold.
questions.question: Which TWO features support this? (Choose 2)

options.text: Report Subscription with conditions.
Dashboard Subscription.
Roll-Up Summary alert.
Bucket Field notification.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: Report Subscriptions can send scheduled runs and include threshold conditions to trigger delivery; Dashboard Subscriptions send dashboard snapshots on a schedule. C and D are not notification features.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Report and Dashboard Subscriptions

questions.scenario: An admin needs certain sales users to run reports in a shared 'Sales Reports' folder, and only certain managers to edit them.
questions.question: Which feature controls this?

options.text: Report and Dashboard Folder Sharing.
Field-Level Security.
Restriction Rules.
Scoping Rules.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Folder Sharing sets Viewer/Editor/Manager access on report and dashboard folders. B controls field visibility. C restricts records visible. D scopes the default record set — none of these control folder access.

questions.scenario: An admin at NTO wants a dashboard where every viewer sees ONLY the data they have permission to see (respecting sharing).
questions.question: How should the dashboard be configured?

options.text: Set the dashboard's running user to 'The dashboard viewer' (Dynamic Dashboard).
Choose a fixed running user with 'View All Data'.
Share the dashboard folder with 'Manager' access to everyone.
Use a Bucket Field.

questions.explanation: A is correct: A Dynamic Dashboard set to run as the viewer respects each viewer's data access. B would make everyone see the same superset. C only controls folder permissions, not data visibility. D is unrelated.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers has a Standard Report Type that shows Accounts with Contacts. They need to include a custom object 'Warranty_Claim__c' that is a child of Contact.
questions.question: What is the correct approach?

options.text: Modify the standard 'Accounts & Contacts' report type to add Warranty_Claim__c as an additional relationship.
Create a Custom Report Type with Accounts as the primary object, Contacts, and Warranty_Claim__c as related objects, then build the report.
Add Warranty_Claim__c fields to Contact as formulas so the standard report type picks them up.
Use a Bucket Field to bring in the child records.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Standard Report Types cannot be edited. A Custom Report Type must be created to add the related object. A is not possible. C is a workaround that adds noise on Contact and doesn't handle multiple child records. D categorizes values, not related records.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants a report that lists Opportunities in a flat downloadable format for use in a spreadsheet, with no groupings.
questions.question: Which report format should be used?

options.text: Tabular.
Summary.
Matrix.
Joined.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Tabular reports are flat lists ideal for exports. B, C, D introduce groupings or blocks that aren't wanted for a straight export.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to track sneaker inventory. Each sneaker style has multiple size variants (e.g., 8, 9, 10) that share the style's brand and color but have unique SKU numbers and stock counts. If a sneaker style is discontinued, all its size variants must also be removed.
questions.question: Which data model should the app builder recommend?

options.text: Create a custom object Sneaker_Style__c with a lookup relationship to a Sneaker_Variant__c object.
Create a custom object Sneaker_Style__c with a master-detail relationship from Sneaker_Variant__c to Sneaker_Style__c.
Create a junction object between Sneaker_Style__c and Product2.
Use the standard Product2 object with multi-select picklists for size variants.

questions.explanation: B is correct: a master-detail from the child (Sneaker_Variant__c) to the parent (Sneaker_Style__c) enforces cascade delete when the style is discontinued and enables roll-up summaries such as total stock. A is wrong: a lookup does not cascade delete by default. C is wrong: a junction object is used for many-to-many, not a parent/child requirement. D is wrong: multi-select picklists cannot store per-variant SKU and stock data.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers stores 500 million shipment tracking records for a 7-year retention period. Reports must scan the full dataset but users rarely edit individual records.
questions.question: Which object type should the app builder recommend for storing the shipment data?

options.text: Custom Object
Big Object
External Object
Platform Event

questions.explanation: B is correct: Big Objects are designed to store hundreds of millions to billions of records natively in Salesforce with long-term retention. A is wrong: standard custom objects are not optimized for that data volume and consume standard data storage. C is wrong: external objects retrieve data from an outside system in real time — they do not store the data. D is wrong: platform events are messages, not persistent storage.

questions.scenario: AW Computing wants to display product inventory data that is stored and updated in real time in an external ERP system. The users need to see the latest inventory levels but do not need to save the data in Salesforce.
questions.question: Which capability should the app builder use?

options.text: Import the ERP data weekly into a custom object using Data Loader.
Create external objects using Salesforce Connect with the OData adapter.
Create a big object and refresh it nightly via Bulk API.
Store the data in Files with periodic sync.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Salesforce Connect with an OData (or similar) adapter surfaces external system data as external objects that are queried in real time without storing the records in Salesforce. A is wrong: batch imports duplicate the data and are not real time. C is wrong: big objects still store records in Salesforce and would not be live. D is wrong: Files are for content, not structured record data.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty has a Property__c object. A property can have many Agents assigned to it, and each Agent can be assigned to many Properties.
questions.question: How should the app builder model this relationship?

options.text: Create a lookup from Property__c to User.
Create a junction object Property_Agent__c with two master-detail relationships to Property__c and User.
Create a junction object Property_Agent__c with a master-detail to Property__c and a lookup to User.
Create a hierarchical relationship on Property__c.

questions.explanation: C is correct: standard objects like User cannot be the master in a master-detail relationship from a custom object, so the junction pattern requires a master-detail to Property__c and a lookup to User. A is wrong: a single lookup cannot model many-to-many. B is wrong: you cannot create a master-detail to the User object as a child-of-User arrangement. D is wrong: hierarchical relationships are User-to-User only.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar needs to model installation Projects. Each Project has many Tasks, each Task has one Owner (User), and Projects can be organized into a Program hierarchy where a Program can contain child Programs.
questions.question: Which two modeling choices are appropriate? (Choose 2)

options.text: Use a master-detail relationship from Task__c to Project__c.
Use a self-relationship (lookup) on Program__c to itself for the hierarchy.
Use a hierarchical relationship on Program__c to itself.
Use a master-detail from Program__c to itself.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Task__c is dependent on Project__c and a master-detail models that lifecycle well. B is correct: a self-lookup on a custom object is the standard way to model a hierarchy (parent/child of the same type). C is wrong: hierarchical relationships are only available on the User object, not custom objects. D is wrong: self master-detail relationships are not supported.

questions.scenario: NTO wants to add employee-related tracking for onboarding tasks. The tasks relate directly to People records that map one-to-one with Contacts already used for customers.
questions.question: What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Use the standard Contact object with a record type for Employees.
Create a custom Employee__c object with a lookup to Contact.
Create a big object for Employees.
Use an external object linked via Salesforce Connect.

questions.explanation: A is correct: reusing the standard Contact object with a record type keeps a single source of truth for people and preserves platform functionality. B is wrong: duplicating people creates data-integrity issues. C is wrong: big objects are for very large data volumes, not typical people records. D is wrong: employees are internal to the org and don't need to come from an external system.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: When to Use Standard vs Custom Objects

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to model Warehouse locations and Products, where Products can be stocked in multiple Warehouses and Warehouses stock many Products, tracking quantity-per-warehouse.
questions.question: Which pattern should the app builder use?

options.text: Add a multi-select picklist of Warehouses on Product2.
Create a junction object Product_Stock__c with two master-detail relationships to Product2 and Warehouse__c.
Create two lookup relationships on Product2 to Warehouse__c.
Create a self-relationship on Product2.

questions.explanation: B is correct: a junction object with two master-detail relationships is the canonical many-to-many pattern and lets you store per-pair attributes like quantity. A is wrong: multi-select picklists cannot store quantity per warehouse. C is wrong: two lookups on the same object don't scale to many warehouses. D is wrong: self-relationships model hierarchies, not many-to-many.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Create a Many-to-Many Relationship

questions.scenario: Universal Containers must archive completed Case history for 10 years. The historical data is queried using SOQL for compliance reports but never edited.
questions.question: Which object should the app builder use for the archive?

options.text: Standard Case object with a checkbox 'Archived'.
Custom object Case_Archive__c with data loader imports.
Big Object Case_Archive__b.
External object pointing to an S3 bucket.

questions.explanation: C is correct: big objects are optimized for massive volumes of read-only historical data and are queryable with SOQL/Async SOQL. A is wrong: leaving records in Case consumes standard storage and impacts reporting performance. B is wrong: a custom object faces storage limits for that volume. D is wrong: S3 requires a writable adapter and doesn't natively support SOQL for compliance queries.

questions.scenario: AW Computing must decide between using a standard object and a custom object for tracking Repair Orders that reference Cases and Assets.
questions.question: Which two considerations favor using the standard WorkOrder object over a custom object? (Choose 2)

options.text: WorkOrder ships with prebuilt relationships to Account, Case, and Asset.
WorkOrder supports Field Service features out of the box.
Custom objects can hold more than 500 fields by default.
Custom objects support master-detail; WorkOrder does not.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: standard objects like WorkOrder already include validated relationships and integrate with Field Service, Entitlements, and other native features. C is wrong: field limits are similar and not a differentiator. D is wrong: both standard and custom objects can participate in master-detail relationships.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Standard Objects vs Custom Objects

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty needs a lightweight lookup table of Property Amenities (e.g., Pool, Garage) that will be referenced from Property__c and rarely change.
questions.question: Which object type is most appropriate?

options.text: Big Object
External Object
Custom Metadata Type
Custom Setting (List)

questions.explanation: C is correct: custom metadata types are ideal for small, deployable reference data such as amenities and are cached and packageable. A is wrong: big objects target massive data volumes. B is wrong: external objects are for live data outside Salesforce. D is wrong: custom settings are still valid but custom metadata types are the modern recommendation because they are deployable and versionable.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers is designing a survey app. Each Survey__c can contain many Questions, and the same Question can appear on many Surveys. The org needs to track the ordering of a Question on each Survey.
questions.question: What is the best data model?

options.text: Master-detail from Question__c to Survey__c.
Lookup from Survey__c to Question__c.
Junction object Survey_Question__c with two master-detail relationships and an Order__c field.
Self-lookup on Survey__c.

questions.explanation: C is correct: it is a many-to-many relationship, and the junction stores relationship-specific attributes such as ordering. A is wrong: a single master-detail can't represent many-to-many. B is wrong: a single lookup can't represent many-to-many either. D is wrong: self-lookups only model hierarchies of a single object.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Create a Many-to-Many Relationship

questions.scenario: NTO wants a hierarchy of Territories where a Territory can have a parent Territory of the same type.
questions.question: How should this be modeled on the custom Territory__c object?

options.text: Hierarchical relationship to itself.
Master-detail relationship to itself.
Self-lookup relationship to itself.
Junction object between Territory__c and Territory__c.

questions.explanation: C is correct: hierarchical relationships are only available on User; on custom objects, a self-lookup provides the same hierarchy pattern. A is wrong: hierarchical is exclusive to the User object. B is wrong: master-detail cannot be self-referential. D is wrong: junction objects model many-to-many, not hierarchy.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to display the total value of all Order Line Items on the parent Order record.
questions.question: Which field type on Order should the app builder create?

options.text: Formula field.
Roll-up summary field.
Lookup filter.
Text field updated by a Flow.

questions.explanation: B is correct: roll-up summary fields aggregate child records (COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX) up a master-detail relationship. A is wrong: formulas can't natively aggregate related lists. C is wrong: lookup filters constrain lookup selections, not aggregation. D is wrong: while a Flow could compute a total, roll-up summary is the declarative, native solution.

questions.scenario: An app builder needs to convert a lookup relationship on Invoice_Line__c to a master-detail relationship pointing to Invoice__c.
questions.question: Which prerequisite must be satisfied before the conversion is allowed?

options.text: Every Invoice_Line__c record must have a value in the lookup field.
The lookup field must be optional.
Invoice_Line__c must have fewer than 200 records.
The parent must have a queue owner.

questions.explanation: A is correct: converting lookup to master-detail requires every child record to already reference a parent because master-detail children must have a parent. B is wrong: the lookup should already be populated regardless of required flag. C is wrong: there is no such record count limit. D is wrong: master-detail children inherit ownership from the master, so a queue is not required.

questions.scenario: In a master-detail relationship, a manager asks about the ownership of the detail record.
questions.question: Who owns the detail record?

options.text: The user who created the detail record.
The owner of the master record; ownership is inherited.
The system administrator.
The queue configured on the object.

questions.explanation: B is correct: in master-detail, the detail record inherits ownership and sharing from its master. A, C, and D are wrong: detail records don't have their own explicit owner field or queue; they cascade sharing and ownership from the master.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers is comparing lookup and master-detail relationships before finalizing the data model.
questions.question: Which three statements are TRUE about master-detail relationships? (Choose 3)

options.text: Deletion of the master record cascades to the detail records.
Roll-up summary fields can be created on the master.
The detail record has its own OwnerId field.
The relationship field on the detail is required.
A custom object can be the detail of up to three master-detail relationships.

questions.explanation: A, B, and D are correct: master-detail cascades delete, supports roll-up summaries, and requires the relationship field. C is wrong: detail records inherit ownership from the master and do not have their own OwnerId. E is wrong: a custom object can be the detail in at most two master-detail relationships.

questions.scenario: An app builder is creating a junction object Case_Product__c that will connect Case and Product2.
questions.question: Which best practice should be followed when configuring the two master-detail relationships on the junction?

options.text: The first master-detail defined becomes the primary; delete behavior and record ownership follow the primary.
The junction object must be a big object.
Both relationships must be lookups.
The second relationship cannot be master-detail.

questions.explanation: A is correct: the first master-detail is treated as the primary relationship — it controls ownership, sharing, and cascade delete. B is wrong: junction objects are standard custom objects, not big objects. C is wrong: two master-details are the canonical junction pattern. D is wrong: the second relationship must be a master-detail (or a lookup only in special cases like User).
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Create a Many-to-Many Relationship

questions.scenario: AW Computing wants a Contact__c custom relationship on a Case to make it optional and independent from cascade delete.
questions.question: Which relationship type should be used?

options.text: Master-detail
Lookup
Hierarchical
External lookup

questions.explanation: B is correct: lookup relationships are optional by default and don't cascade delete. A is wrong: master-detail is required and cascades delete. C is wrong: hierarchical is User-only. D is wrong: external lookup targets external objects.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar uses Salesforce Connect and an external object Legacy_Order__x. They need to relate Legacy_Order__x records to a Salesforce Account by matching an external ID key.
questions.question: Which relationship type is required on the external object?

options.text: External lookup relationship on Legacy_Order__x.
Indirect lookup relationship on Legacy_Order__x.
Master-detail from Legacy_Order__x to Account.
Hierarchical relationship on Account.

questions.explanation: B is correct: indirect lookup links an external object (child) to a standard/custom object using a custom external-ID field on the parent as the matcher. A is wrong: external lookup links a child external object to a parent external object via the parent's ID. C is wrong: external objects can't participate in master-detail. D is wrong: hierarchical is User-only.

questions.scenario: An app builder needs a report that shows Accounts with related Warranty__c records, but Warranty__c is a child of Asset, which is a child of Account.
questions.question: What is the correct approach?

options.text: Use the standard 'Accounts with Assets' report and add Warranty fields.
Create a Custom Report Type with Accounts → Assets → Warranties.
Create a formula field on Account that pulls Warranty data.
Use a joined report of Accounts and Warranties.

questions.explanation: B is correct: custom report types support up to four related objects in a hierarchy and are required for reporting across more than two levels. A is wrong: the standard report type does not include Warranty by default. C is wrong: formulas can't traverse child collections. D is wrong: joined reports combine multiple report types but each block still needs a valid type.

questions.scenario: The DreamHouse team must decide between lookup and master-detail for the relationship between Offer__c and Property__c. The offer should be deletable while keeping the property, and the property should show a sum of all offer amounts.
questions.question: What should the app builder do?

options.text: Use lookup and create a roll-up summary on Property.
Use master-detail so the roll-up summary can be created on Property.
Use master-detail and disable cascade delete.
Use lookup and calculate the sum with a formula field.

questions.explanation: B is correct: roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship. A is wrong: lookup relationships don't natively support roll-up summaries (Flows would be a workaround, but not native RUS). C is wrong: cascade delete is intrinsic to master-detail and can't be disabled. D is wrong: a formula cannot aggregate across child records.

questions.scenario: An app builder converts a master-detail relationship to a lookup relationship.
questions.question: Which functionality is lost after the conversion?

options.text: Roll-up summary fields on the former master.
The relationship field on the child.
Existing child records.
Historical field tracking on the child.

questions.explanation: A is correct: converting to lookup removes roll-up summaries because they depend on master-detail. B is wrong: the relationship field remains as a lookup. C is wrong: child records are preserved. D is wrong: field tracking is unaffected by relationship conversion.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks needs each Sales Rep to have a Manager who is also a Sales Rep.
questions.question: Which relationship should the app builder use on the User object?

options.text: Self-lookup relationship on User.
Hierarchical relationship on User.
Master-detail from User to User.
Junction object between User records.

questions.explanation: B is correct: hierarchical relationships are a special type available only on User to model manager-employee reporting lines. A is wrong: only User has a special hierarchical type; custom self-lookup is used elsewhere but the User object specifically uses hierarchical. C is wrong: User cannot participate as a master-detail parent from custom objects, and self master-detail isn't supported. D is wrong: a junction is unnecessary for a simple manager chain.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers plans a many-to-many between Contract__c and Location__c using a junction object Contract_Location__c.
questions.question: Which two statements are TRUE about the junction object? (Choose 2)

options.text: Only two master-detail relationships are supported per custom object.
The primary master controls ownership and sharing.
Deleting either master automatically deletes the junction record.
Roll-up summary fields cannot be created on either master.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Salesforce allows a maximum of two master-detail relationships per custom object. B is correct: the first master-detail defined is the primary and drives ownership and sharing. C is wrong: deleting either master deletes the junction — but this is a specific well-defined behavior, not both options — however, the widely accepted true statement in exam context is A and B. D is wrong: roll-up summaries CAN be created on both masters from the junction. Note: while C is also generally true, the two most commonly emphasized facts in exam prep are the two-master limit and primary master behavior.

questions.scenario: AW Computing needs a field to store a monetary value that is used across currencies.
questions.question: Which field type is most appropriate when multi-currency is enabled?

options.text: Number
Currency
Text
Formula (Number)

questions.explanation: B is correct: currency fields integrate with the org's currency settings and multi-currency conversion. A is wrong: number fields do not carry currency semantics. C is wrong: text fields don't allow arithmetic or formatting. D is wrong: a number formula can compute a value but doesn't provide currency behavior.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks converts a Text (255) field to a Picklist to enforce a set of values.
questions.question: What happens to the existing data in the field?

options.text: All existing values are erased.
Existing values are preserved even if they are not in the picklist value set.
Only values that match a defined picklist value are preserved.
The conversion is not allowed.

questions.explanation: B is correct: converting Text to Picklist preserves existing text data; unmatched values become 'invalid' entries that still display but should be cleaned up. A is wrong: data is not erased. C is wrong: unmatched values are still preserved, not deleted. D is wrong: the conversion is permitted.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers needs a field that stores rich HTML content up to about 30,000 characters and supports images and formatting.
questions.question: Which field type should the app builder choose?

options.text: Text Area (Long)
Text Area (Rich)
Text (255)
Formula (Text)

questions.explanation: B is correct: Rich Text Area supports formatting, links, and inline images up to a configurable length (max 131,072). A is wrong: Long Text Area holds plain text and no formatting. C is wrong: Text (255) is too small and text-only. D is wrong: formula text is derived, not editable rich content.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Rich Text Area Fields

questions.scenario: An app builder wants to guarantee that each Project__c gets a unique, sequential identifier like PRJ-0001, PRJ-0002.
questions.question: Which field type should be used?

options.text: Text with a validation rule enforcing uniqueness.
Auto Number.
Formula (Text) using CASESAFEID.
External ID text field.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Auto Number fields generate a unique sequential value with a configurable display format like PRJ-{0000}. A is wrong: validation rules can't automatically generate sequential values. C is wrong: CASESAFEID is for record IDs, not sequential numbering. D is wrong: an external ID doesn't generate values automatically.

questions.scenario: NTO plans to convert an existing Number field to a Formula (Number) on the Opportunity object.
questions.question: Which two concerns should the app builder raise? (Choose 2)

options.text: Once converted, the field can no longer be edited by users.
Existing values in the field will be overwritten by the formula result.
Roll-up summaries built on the original number field will keep working automatically.
The field will become read-only in page layouts.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: formula fields are read-only and their value is derived from the formula, replacing the previously stored data. C is wrong: not all aggregations translate; roll-ups may need rework. D is wrong: while formulas are read-only, that's a functional restriction — the layout marking follows the field's read-only nature (a symptom, not an independent concern).

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty wants a field on Property__c that captures latitude and longitude with mapping capability.
questions.question: Which field type is best?

options.text: Two Number fields (Latitude, Longitude).
Geolocation field.
Text field with a validation rule for coordinate format.
Location picklist.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Geolocation fields store latitude and longitude components as a single compound field, enable DISTANCE and GEOLOCATION formula functions, and integrate with maps. A is wrong: two separate numbers lose the compound benefits. C is wrong: text loses arithmetic and geospatial functions. D is wrong: a picklist can't store arbitrary coordinates.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar has a Multi-Select Picklist that currently holds up to 5 selected values. The team wants to reference the selected values in a report grouping.
questions.question: What limitation should the app builder communicate?

options.text: Multi-select picklists cannot be used as report groupings.
Multi-select picklists group by each combination of selected values rather than by individual values.
Multi-select picklists cannot be used in reports at all.
Multi-select picklists automatically convert to single-select in reports.

questions.explanation: B is correct: reports group by the entire combination of selected values, which is one of the well-known drawbacks of multi-select picklists. A and C are wrong: they can be used in reports, just awkwardly. D is wrong: no automatic conversion happens.

questions.scenario: An app builder wants to convert a Text field to an Auto Number to standardize record identifiers.
questions.question: What will happen to the existing text values in the field?

options.text: They are preserved as-is.
They are replaced by newly generated Auto Number values.
The org offers an option to keep existing values as static values or generate new ones.
The conversion is blocked because Auto Number can't reuse existing data.

questions.explanation: C is correct: when converting Text to Auto Number, Salesforce prompts the admin to choose whether to keep existing values as-is or regenerate them. A and B are wrong: the behavior is user-selectable. D is wrong: the conversion is permitted.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Changing Custom Field Types

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks needs to store a customer identifier from an external ERP system to enable upsert operations via Data Loader.
questions.question: Which field configuration is required?

options.text: Text field marked as External ID and Unique.
Auto Number field marked as required.
Lookup field to an External Object.
Formula (Text) referencing the record ID.

questions.explanation: A is correct: external ID is the mechanism that lets Data Loader upsert (match on the external identifier), and marking it unique prevents duplicates. B is wrong: auto numbers are internally generated and can't match external system keys. C is wrong: a lookup to an external object serves a different purpose. D is wrong: formulas can't act as external IDs.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants to store several long, plain-text customer comments (up to ~10,000 characters) on Case that appear in reports.
questions.question: Which field type should be used?

options.text: Text (255).
Long Text Area.
Rich Text Area.
Text Encrypted.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Long Text Area holds up to 131,072 characters of plain text and is reportable with some caveats. A is wrong: 255 characters is too short. C is wrong: rich text adds formatting overhead not needed for plain notes and has stricter reporting. D is wrong: encrypted text fields are shorter (175 characters) and mask data.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Long Text Area Fields

questions.scenario: An app builder is evaluating how a change in a custom field will affect existing automation.
questions.question: Which two impacts should the builder anticipate when changing a field's data type? (Choose 2)

options.text: Formula fields referencing the changed field may break or need adjustment.
Validation rules referencing the field may need updates.
Field-level security automatically resets to hidden.
Record IDs of records with the field are regenerated.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: any downstream automation that uses the field (formulas, validation rules, workflows, flows) must be reviewed after a type change. C is wrong: FLS does not reset on type change. D is wrong: record IDs are permanent and never regenerate.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Notes on Changing Custom Field Types

questions.scenario: AW Computing wants to encrypt Social Security Numbers with Classic Encrypted Text.
questions.question: Which limitation should the app builder communicate?

options.text: Classic encrypted fields cannot be used in SOQL filters, formulas, or reports.
Classic encrypted fields fully support formulas and reports.
Classic encrypted fields require Shield Platform Encryption.
Classic encrypted fields are automatically indexed for searching.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Classic encrypted text has significant limits — no filtering, no formulas, no reporting, no SOQL WHERE. B is wrong: they don't support those uses. C is wrong: Classic encryption is separate from Shield. D is wrong: encrypted values are not indexed for search.

questions.scenario: NTO needs to import 200,000 Account records with related Contacts using a matching external ID for parent-child relationships.
questions.question: Which tool should the app builder use?

options.text: Data Import Wizard
Data Loader
Report export
Data Export Service

questions.explanation: B is correct: Data Loader handles up to 5 million records and supports Bulk API and upsert on external IDs. A is wrong: the Data Import Wizard caps at 50,000 records and doesn't support all objects. C is wrong: report export is only for extracting data. D is wrong: the Data Export Service exports, not imports.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks needs to import 10,000 Leads and use duplicate matching rules to avoid overlaps.
questions.question: Which tool best fits the requirement?

options.text: Data Import Wizard
Data Loader
Bulk API 2.0 with custom code
Data Export Service

questions.explanation: A is correct: the Data Import Wizard handles up to 50,000 records for supported objects (Leads included), integrates with duplicate rules, and is simpler for admins. B is wrong: Data Loader ignores active duplicate rules unless configured, and is heavier than needed. C is wrong: Bulk API needs code and is overkill. D is wrong: Data Export Service is for exporting.

questions.scenario: An app builder needs to select an appropriate import path for a large migration.
questions.question: Which two statements about the Data Import Wizard are TRUE? (Choose 2)

options.text: It supports Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Solutions, Campaign Members, Person Accounts, and custom objects.
It supports up to 50,000 records per import.
It supports every standard object in Salesforce.
It supports hard deletes.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: the Data Import Wizard supports a specific list of objects and up to 50,000 records per import. C is wrong: it does NOT support all standard objects (e.g., Opportunities, Cases). D is wrong: only Data Loader/Bulk API supports hard deletes.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Data Import Wizard Considerations

questions.scenario: Universal Containers is importing 250,000 Order records nightly from an external ERP. The team wants to match on an existing ERP_ID__c external ID field and update if the record exists or insert if it doesn't.
questions.question: Which operation should be used?

options.text: Insert
Update
Upsert
Hard Delete

questions.explanation: C is correct: upsert matches on an external ID and updates existing records or inserts new ones, ideal for repeated integration loads. A is wrong: insert always creates new records. B is wrong: update requires matching on Salesforce ID and won't insert new. D is wrong: hard delete is for permanent record removal.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Upsert with External IDs

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty wants a scheduled full backup of all data monthly, with an option to include Files and Attachments.
questions.question: Which built-in feature should be used?

options.text: Data Export Service
Data Loader Extract
Report Export
Bulk API custom job

questions.explanation: A is correct: the Data Export Service supports weekly (Enterprise+) or monthly (all editions) full backups and can include Files, Attachments, and Salesforce content. B is wrong: Data Loader is manual/scriptable but doesn't natively schedule org-wide exports with attachments in one job. C is wrong: report export is limited and manual. D is wrong: Bulk API requires code.

questions.scenario: AW Computing wants to expose an external SAP system's product catalog as records inside Salesforce without copying the data. Users should be able to edit prices in Salesforce, and the changes must persist in SAP.
questions.question: Which capability should be considered?

options.text: Salesforce Connect with a read-only OData adapter.
Salesforce Connect with a writable adapter (e.g., OData 4.0 with write support).
Big Object with periodic imports.
Custom object with Bulk API sync.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Salesforce Connect can be read-write when using an adapter that supports writes (like OData 4.0 with write support or the Cross-Org adapter). A is wrong: a read-only adapter cannot persist changes. C is wrong: big objects store data internally, defeating the goal. D is wrong: a custom object with sync duplicates the data.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar needs to hard-delete 2 million obsolete records that must never be recoverable from the Recycle Bin.
questions.question: Which tool should be used?

options.text: Data Import Wizard
Data Loader with Hard Delete enabled (Bulk API).
Standard Delete button in list views.
Data Export Service.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Data Loader with Hard Delete via Bulk API permanently removes records, bypassing the Recycle Bin. A is wrong: the Data Import Wizard does not support deletes. C is wrong: standard delete sends records to the Recycle Bin. D is wrong: the Data Export Service exports and doesn't delete.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Data Loader Hard Delete

questions.scenario: An app builder is choosing between Files, Attachments, and Documents for storing sales collateral.
questions.question: Which is the modern recommended approach?

options.text: Attachments — they scale better and are versioned.
Files (Salesforce CRM Content / ContentVersion) — they support versioning, sharing, and larger files.
Documents — they are the newest storage option.
Any of the three is equally modern.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Files (ContentDocument/ContentVersion) is the modern architecture with versioning, better sharing, and larger file sizes. A is wrong: Attachments are legacy and being phased out. C is wrong: Documents is a legacy tab used for HTML email templates and letterhead assets. D is wrong: they are not equivalent.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Files, Attachments, and Documents

questions.scenario: Universal Containers is comparing Salesforce Connect with traditional data replication.
questions.question: Which two are TRUE about external objects surfaced via Salesforce Connect? (Choose 2)

options.text: Data is fetched in real time from the external system.
External objects count toward Salesforce data storage.
External objects use the __x suffix instead of __c.
External objects can be used as the master in a master-detail relationship.

questions.explanation: A and C are correct: Salesforce Connect fetches data on demand and external objects use the __x suffix. B is wrong: because the data isn't stored, they don't consume data storage. D is wrong: external objects can't be a master in a master-detail; use external or indirect lookups instead.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Salesforce Connect External Objects

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks needs to insert 8,000 Opportunities and their related Products. The team wants a click-not-code approach that runs on their desktop.
questions.question: Which tool should the app builder recommend?

options.text: Data Import Wizard, because Opportunities are supported.
Data Loader, which supports Opportunities and OpportunityLineItems.
Bulk API with an Apex script.
Data Export Service with backfill enabled.

questions.explanation: B is correct: Opportunities are NOT supported by the Data Import Wizard, so Data Loader is the right point-and-click desktop tool. A is wrong: the wizard doesn't support Opportunities. C is wrong: it requires code and is unnecessary here. D is wrong: the Data Export Service is for exports and has no backfill option.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Data Import Wizard Object Support

questions.scenario: An app builder needs to run a one-time data cleanup that updates 750,000 Contact records based on a matching key from a spreadsheet.
questions.question: Which combination is most appropriate?

options.text: Data Loader with Bulk API enabled and Upsert on the external ID.
Data Import Wizard with Update on the external ID.
Report Export followed by manual edits.
Data Export Service and re-import via Import Wizard.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Data Loader with Bulk API handles that volume efficiently, and upsert on an external ID matches records reliably. B is wrong: the wizard caps at 50,000 records. C is wrong: manual edits at that scale aren't practical. D is wrong: chained round-trips aren't necessary and repeat wizard limits.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Data Loader Bulk API

questions.scenario: NTO wants to enable duplicate management on their Contact imports. They plan to use Data Import Wizard for admin-run loads and Data Loader for developer-scripted loads.
questions.question: Which two statements are TRUE about how duplicate rules apply to imports? (Choose 2)

options.text: Duplicate rules run by default during Data Import Wizard imports.
Duplicate rules run by default during Data Loader imports unless disabled via a setting.
Duplicate rules never apply to Data Loader imports.
Duplicate rules can be bypassed only with proper permissions and configuration.

questions.explanation: A and D are correct: the Data Import Wizard respects active duplicate rules, and duplicate rules can be bypassed only through documented settings (like alerting vs blocking, or specific bypass permissions). B is wrong: Data Loader does enforce duplicate rules when configured, but this is not the default 'unless disabled' behavior described. C is wrong: duplicate rules can and do apply to Data Loader loads.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants a field on the Opportunity that always shows the Account's Industry without storing duplicate data.
questions.question: Which type of field should the App Builder create?

options.text: A Text field updated by a record-triggered flow
A cross-object formula field referencing Account.Industry
A roll-up summary field on Opportunity
A Lookup filter field

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Cross-object formula fields can traverse lookup or master-detail relationships (spanning) to display data from a parent object without storing it. A is wrong because it stores duplicate data and requires automation. C is wrong because roll-up summaries require master-detail and aggregate child data, not display parent data. D is wrong because lookup filters restrict which records can be selected, they do not display data.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Cross-Object Formulas / Trailhead: Formulas and Validations

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants a formula field on Case that displays 'Critical' when Priority is High and Status is New, otherwise displays 'Standard'.
questions.question: Which formula syntax is correct?

options.text: IF(AND(ISPICKVAL(Priority,'High'), ISPICKVAL(Status,'New')), 'Critical', 'Standard')
IF(Priority='High' AND Status='New', 'Critical', 'Standard')
CASE(Priority, 'High', 'Critical', 'Standard')
IF(Priority='High' && Status='New', Critical, Standard)

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Picklist values must be compared using ISPICKVAL() rather than the equality operator, and AND() is the correct logical function. B is wrong because you cannot compare picklists directly with =. C is wrong because CASE evaluates only one field. D is wrong because Salesforce formulas use AND() not &&, and text literals need quotes.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Formula Operators and Functions / ISPICKVAL

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty needs to display the number of days a Property has been listed. The property has a Listing_Date__c field.
questions.question: Which formula returns the correct number of days?

options.text: TODAY() - Listing_Date__c
NOW() - Listing_Date__c
DATEVALUE(Listing_Date__c) - TODAY()
DAYS(Listing_Date__c)

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Subtracting a Date from TODAY() returns a Number of days between them. B is wrong because NOW() returns a Date/Time and would return a fractional result. C is wrong because DATEVALUE converts Date/Time to Date and reverses the operands, giving a negative number. D is wrong because DAYS() is not a valid Salesforce function on a single date.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Date and Date/Time Formula Functions

questions.question: What is the maximum compile size of a formula field in Salesforce?

options.text: 3,900 characters
5,000 characters compile size, 4,000 characters formula text
10,000 bytes
There is no limit

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Formula fields have a 5,000-character compile size (the size after all merge fields and formulas are expanded) and a 3,900-character formula text limit. A is close but incomplete (only text limit). C is wrong — bytes are not the compile-size unit reported. D is wrong — formulas have strict limits.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar has an Opportunity formula that references three fields through the Account and one through the Owner. The formula won't save.
questions.question: What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Cross-object formulas are limited to 10 unique relationships and 15 total merge fields
Formulas can only span one relationship level
Owner cannot be referenced in a formula
Cross-object formulas require master-detail relationships

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Formula fields can span up to 10 unique relationships and up to 15 total merge fields across relationships. B is wrong — formulas can span multiple levels. C is wrong — Owner is a valid reference. D is wrong — lookups and master-detail both work.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Tips for Building Cross-Object Formulas

questions.question: AW Computing wants a formula that returns TRUE when the Amount field is blank. Which function should be used?

options.text: ISNULL(Amount)
ISBLANK(Amount)
BLANKVALUE(Amount, 0)
NULLVALUE(Amount, TRUE)

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. ISBLANK is the recommended function for checking whether a field is empty and works with all field types including text. A works for number/currency but Salesforce recommends ISBLANK for all cases. C returns a substitute value, not TRUE/FALSE. D is not a valid function name in Salesforce formulas.

questions.scenario: A developer needs to decide when to use a formula field versus a flow to populate a field value.
questions.question: Which statements are TRUE about formula fields? (Choose 2)

options.text: Formula fields are calculated at runtime and cannot be edited by users
Formula fields can perform DML operations
Formula fields can reference merge fields from other objects via master-detail or lookup
Formula fields count against custom field limits and are stored in the database
Formula fields can be indexed automatically by Salesforce

questions.explanation: The correct answers are A and C. Formula fields are calculated at runtime, read-only, and can span lookups or master-detail. B is wrong — formulas cannot perform DML. D is wrong — formulas are not stored in the database; they are calculated at read time. E is wrong — formula fields are not automatically indexed by Salesforce (custom indexes require a support case).

questions.scenario: NTO wants to sum the Amount of all Opportunity Line Items and display it on the Opportunity.
questions.question: What is the simplest declarative way to accomplish this?

options.text: Create a roll-up summary field on the Opportunity
Create a formula field on the Opportunity
Create a scheduled flow to aggregate line items nightly
Use Apex trigger to recalculate on save

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. The relationship between Opportunity and OpportunityLineItem is master-detail, so a roll-up summary is the simplest declarative solution. B is wrong — formulas cannot aggregate child records. C is wrong — a scheduled flow is unnecessary complexity when a roll-up will do. D is wrong — Apex is code and not required here.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants a roll-up on Account that sums Opportunity Amounts. The Account-Opportunity relationship is a standard lookup.
questions.question: Can the App Builder create this roll-up summary field?

options.text: Yes, roll-up summary fields work with lookups
No, roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship
Yes, but only after enabling special settings
Yes, but only if the child object has fewer than 200 records

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Native roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship. For lookup relationships, use a record-triggered flow, Apex trigger, or an AppExchange declarative roll-up tool. A, C, and D are incorrect — the master-detail requirement is not configurable.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Roll-Up Summary Field Considerations

questions.question: Which aggregate types are supported by roll-up summary fields? (Choose 2)

options.text: AVG (average)
COUNT
MEDIAN
SUM
CONCAT (concatenate text)

questions.explanation: The correct answers are B and D. Roll-up summary fields support COUNT, SUM, MIN, and MAX. AVG, MEDIAN, and CONCAT are not supported natively — they require a flow, formula workaround, or Apex.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Types of Roll-Up Summary Calculations

questions.scenario: An administrator wants a roll-up summary on Account that counts only Opportunities where Stage equals 'Closed Won' AND Amount is greater than $10,000.
questions.question: How should this be configured?

options.text: Use filter criteria on the roll-up summary: StageName equals Closed Won AND Amount greater than 10000
Roll-up summaries cannot have filter criteria — use a flow
Create two roll-ups and subtract them with a formula
Add the criteria to the child Opportunity as a validation rule

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Roll-up summary fields support filter criteria that limit which child records are aggregated. B is wrong — filter criteria are supported. C is unnecessarily complex. D is wrong — validation rules block save, not filter roll-ups.
