Report Chart
News

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. The Recommendations component surfaces context-aware next-best actions (based on Next Best Action strategies or Einstein). A shows stage progress. C embeds a report chart. D shows news items about the account (Account Insights).
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Einstein Next Best Action & Recommendations Component

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants to display a static HTML-formatted announcement, including a bulleted list and a link, on the Home page for all users.
questions.question: Which standard component should the admin use?

options.text: Rich Text
Chatter Feed
Report Chart
Related Record

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. The Rich Text component allows admins to add formatted static content (bullets, links, styling) declaratively on any Lightning page. B is for feed posts. C is for report charts. D is for related record fields.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks has a custom LWC that appears in the Lightning App Builder, but the admin needs to hide it from users whose Region field is not 'North America'.
questions.question: How can the admin restrict the component's visibility?

options.text: Modify the LWC's Apex controller to check the user's Region
Set a Component Visibility filter on the component in App Builder using the User's Region field
Assign a permission set that hides the component
Set the component's isExposed attribute to false

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Component Visibility filters in App Builder can evaluate the running user's fields (including custom fields like Region), so admins can declaratively control which users see the component. A is programmatic overkill. C isn't how component visibility works. D would remove the component from App Builder entirely.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Component Visibility Rules — User Fields

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are valid page targets for a Lightning Web Component to be used in Lightning App Builder? (Choose 2)

options.text: lightning__RecordPage
lightning__HomePage
lightning__CompactLayout
lightning__PageLayout

questions.explanation: The correct answers are A and B. lightning__RecordPage, lightning__HomePage, and lightning__AppPage are valid Lightning App Builder page targets, along with lightning__RecordAction, lightning__Tab, lightning__FlowScreen, and Experience Cloud targets. C and D are not valid target names — compact layouts and page layouts aren't LWC targets.
questions.reference: Salesforce Developer Docs: Configure a Component for Lightning App Builder

questions.scenario: NTO's admin needs a UI element that combines data from three unrelated objects, applies a custom sort algorithm, and renders a heatmap visualization. No standard component or existing app can do this.
questions.question: What should the admin do?

options.text: Build it declaratively using Dynamic Forms and visibility rules
Ask a developer to build a custom Lightning Web Component that can be dropped into the record page via App Builder
Use the Rich Text component
Use the Recommendations component

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. When a UI requirement can't be met with standard components, Dynamic Forms, Path, related lists, or App Builder configuration, admins should partner with a developer to build a custom LWC. A, C, and D cannot deliver the required cross-object logic and custom visualization.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: When to Use Custom Lightning Components

questions.question: Which statement about Lightning Web Components (LWC) vs Aura Components is TRUE?

options.text: Aura is Salesforce's modern, recommended framework and LWC is legacy
LWC is Salesforce's modern, standards-based framework and is recommended for new development over Aura
Both LWC and Aura components cannot be dropped onto Lightning App Builder pages
Only Aura components can be used on Lightning record pages

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. LWC is Salesforce's modern component framework built on web standards; it's the recommended framework for new component development. Aura is still supported but LWC is preferred for performance and standards alignment. A is reversed. C is false — both frameworks can be exposed to App Builder via targets. D is false — LWC works fine on record pages.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Lightning Web Components vs Aura

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty is building a new customer-facing site in Experience Cloud that needs to load fast, use modern web standards, and support custom LWCs without Aura dependencies.
questions.question: Which Experience Cloud template family should DreamHouse Realty choose?

options.text: Aura-based Customer Service template
Lightning Web Runtime (LWR) template
Visualforce Sites
Salesforce Tabs + Visualforce

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. LWR (Lightning Web Runtime) templates are the modern, performance-oriented Experience Cloud sites built entirely on LWC — fast page loads, standards-based, no Aura runtime. A uses Aura and is not recommended for new performance-critical sites. C and D are legacy site technologies.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: LWR Templates for Experience Cloud

questions.question: When would an App Builder need to engage a developer instead of solving a UI requirement declaratively?

options.text: To add a report chart to a record page
To hide a field on a record page based on a field value
To build a custom UI element that no standard component, Dynamic Forms, or Path can provide
To add a quick action to create a related record

questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. A, B, and D are all declarative — Report Chart is a standard component, field visibility can be done with Dynamic Forms/Component Visibility, and Quick Actions handle related record creation. Only C — a truly custom UI element beyond declarative reach — requires a developer to build a custom LWC or Aura component.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Declarative vs Programmatic Development

questions.scenario: Universal Containers has a custom LWC that a developer built. The admin wants to place this component on the Utility Bar of a Lightning App.
questions.question: What must be true for this to work?

options.text: The LWC must have lightning__UtilityBar exposed as a target in its .js-meta.xml
The Utility Bar only supports standard components
The LWC must be converted to an Aura component
The LWC must be added to the compact layout

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. The LWC's .js-meta.xml must expose lightning__UtilityBar as a target. B is false — custom components can appear in the utility bar. C is false — LWC works fine in utility bars. D isn't a related concept.
questions.reference: Salesforce Developer Docs: LWC Targets — Utility Bar

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants field reps using the Salesforce mobile app to see a streamlined summary card at the top of each Account record — just Name, Phone, and Rating.
questions.question: Which layout controls the fields displayed on the mobile record card?

options.text: Page Layout
Compact Layout
Search Layout
Mobile Layout

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Compact layouts drive the fields shown at the top of records in the Salesforce mobile app (as well as highlights panel and hover cards in Lightning Experience). A controls the rest of the record body. C controls list view/search columns. D isn't a specific standard layout type in this context.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Compact Layouts on Mobile

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar's field service technicians need to work in areas without connectivity. The admin needs to prime a subset of Case, Account, and Work Order records so they're available offline in the Salesforce mobile app.
questions.question: Which tool should the admin use?

options.text: Salesforce Files Sync
Briefcase Builder
Mobile Publisher
Data Loader

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Briefcase Builder is the declarative tool for defining what records are cached (primed) on the Salesforce mobile app for offline access — including filters, priorities, and assignments. A is for syncing files. C repackages the mobile app for external branding. D imports/exports data, not offline priming.

questions.scenario: AW Computing wants specific quick actions to appear only in the Salesforce mobile app for Opportunity records — not on the desktop record page.
questions.question: How can the admin accomplish this?

options.text: Actions defined for mobile are automatically hidden from desktop

Set the action's page layout section to include the action only in the mobile-only Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions area, then use Dynamic Actions with Form Factor = Phone visibility rule in the highlights panel
Create a separate 'mobile' record type
Mobile-only actions can only be delivered via a Lightning Component

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. The clearest approach in modern Lightning is to use Dynamic Actions in the highlights panel with Form Factor = Phone visibility filters, so the action only renders on mobile. A is false — actions on a shared list don't automatically discriminate by device. C isn't a mobile mechanism. D is not required — declarative actions with visibility rules work.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Dynamic Actions with Form Factor Rules

questions.question: Which TWO statements about the Salesforce mobile app navigation menu are TRUE? (Choose 2)

options.text: The mobile navigation menu is configured per app in App Manager, using the app's Navigation Items
The mobile navigation menu is always identical to the desktop navigation bar and cannot be customized
Users can access the mobile navigation via a menu icon (typically the bottom navigation or side menu)
Only developers can configure the mobile navigation menu

questions.explanation: The correct answers are A and C. Lightning Apps configured in App Manager drive both the desktop navigation bar AND the mobile app navigation for that app; admins can reorder items and pick different tabs. The mobile menu is reachable via the bottom bar or side menu. B is false — the menu can be customized per app. D is false — this is admin territory.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Mobile App Navigation and Lightning Apps

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty's admin created a Lightning record page for the Property object with a large embedded Report Chart and multiple visibility rules. Users on mobile report the page renders slowly.
questions.question: Which declarative approach best addresses this?

options.text: Rebuild the page in Aura for better mobile performance
Create a separate, streamlined Lightning record page and assign it to the Phone form factor via the Activation dialog
Move the report chart to the compact layout
Disable Dynamic Forms globally

questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Lightning Pages can be assigned separately to Desktop and Phone form factors. Building a phone-optimized version (lighter, fewer heavy components like a report chart) and assigning it via the Activation dialog gives the best mobile experience. A is regressive. C isn't valid — you can't put a report chart on a compact layout. D is unnecessary and unrelated to performance.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Assign Lightning Pages to Form Factors

questions.question: Which statement about global vs object-specific actions on the Salesforce mobile app is TRUE?

options.text: Global actions are available from anywhere in the app; object-specific actions appear on that object's record page and in the object's list view
Only global actions are available on mobile
Object-specific actions cannot include Create a Record type
Both types are only available on desktop

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. On mobile (as on desktop), global actions surface from the '+'/action menu app-wide, while object-specific actions are contextual to that object's record page and list. B is false — object-specific actions are absolutely available on mobile. C is false — that's a common object-specific action type. D is false — both are mobile-supported.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Global vs Object-Specific Actions

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants field technicians using the Salesforce mobile app in remote locations to be able to view a specific set of Work Order records and update fields on them, even with no connectivity.
questions.question: Which combination of features should the admin implement?

options.text: Briefcase Builder to define offline records and mobile actions/pages configured for edit
Mobile Publisher to enable offline
Data Loader jobs scheduled for the mobile users
Custom LWC with local storage; no other configuration required

questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Briefcase Builder declaratively primes a defined set of records for offline availability in the Salesforce mobile app, and the standard mobile experience supports viewing and editing those records offline (with sync when back online). B rebrands the app but isn't the offline mechanism. C runs server-side and doesn't help offline mobile. D is programmatic and unnecessary when Briefcase covers it declaratively.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Briefcase Builder & Mobile Offline

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks has a small team of three developers who need isolated environments to build custom objects and Apex classes without touching production data.
questions.question: Which sandbox type is best suited for each developer to build and unit test new metadata?

options.text: Full sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
Developer sandbox
Developer Pro sandbox

questions.explanation: Developer sandbox is the correct answer. It is a lightweight environment intended for coding and configuration by a single developer, includes 200 MB of storage, and can be refreshed once per day. A (Full) is overkill and expensive because it copies all production data. B (Partial Copy) requires a sandbox template and 5-day refresh interval—too heavy for individual dev work. D (Developer Pro) is valid but larger (1 GB); Developer sandboxes are the standard choice for individual devs unless the extra storage is required.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Sandbox Types and Licenses

questions.scenario: Universal Containers needs a sandbox for User Acceptance Testing (UAT) that contains a representative sample of production data but does not need a full copy. The QA lead wants to control which data is copied using a sandbox template.
questions.question: Which sandbox type meets these requirements?

options.text: Developer sandbox
Developer Pro sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
Full sandbox

questions.explanation: Partial Copy sandbox is correct. It supports sandbox templates (which define which objects and how many records to copy), includes up to 5 GB of storage, and refreshes every 5 days—ideal for UAT with sample data. A and B (Developer / Developer Pro) copy metadata only, no data. D (Full) also supports templates but is more expensive and refreshes only every 29 days—unnecessary when a sample suffices.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty is preparing to run a full regression test and staging rehearsal that must mirror production exactly, including all data and Chatter feeds.
questions.question: Which sandbox type should the release manager use?

options.text: Developer Pro sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
Full sandbox
Developer sandbox

questions.explanation: Full sandbox is correct. It is the only sandbox that is a complete replica of production, including all data (with optional Chatter feeds and history), and is designed for staging, performance testing, and full regression. It refreshes every 29 days. A and D copy metadata only. B (Partial Copy) copies a sample of data, not the full production dataset—insufficient for full regression.

questions.scenario: The AW Computing admin team is comparing sandbox types before purchasing additional environments.
questions.question: Which two sandbox types support sandbox templates for selecting which data to copy? (Choose 2)

options.text: Developer
Developer Pro
Partial Copy
Full

questions.explanation: C (Partial Copy) and D (Full) both support sandbox templates. Templates let admins choose which objects—and for Partial Copy, how many records—are seeded into the sandbox. A (Developer) and B (Developer Pro) copy metadata only and do not include any production data, so templates do not apply.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Create or Edit Sandbox Templates

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar's admin wants to refresh a Full sandbox that was created 20 days ago.
questions.question: What is the minimum refresh interval for a Full sandbox?

options.text: 1 day
5 days
29 days
It can be refreshed any time

questions.explanation: C is correct. Full sandboxes have a minimum refresh interval of 29 days. A applies to Developer and Developer Pro (1 day), B applies to Partial Copy (5 days), and D is incorrect because every sandbox type has a documented refresh floor.

questions.scenario: NTO's DevOps lead wants developers working on parallel features to each have their own environment that includes 1 GB of storage but no production data.
questions.question: Which sandbox type is the best fit?

options.text: Developer sandbox
Developer Pro sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
Full sandbox

questions.explanation: Developer Pro is correct. It provides 1 GB of storage (vs. 200 MB for a standard Developer sandbox), refreshes daily, and copies metadata only—no data. A has only 200 MB storage. C and D both copy production data, which is not needed here.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Sandbox Types and Licenses

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks refreshed its Partial Copy sandbox on the 1st of the month for UAT. The QA team found a data issue and wants to refresh again 3 days later.
questions.question: What will happen?

options.text: The refresh will succeed immediately
The refresh will be queued until the 5-day minimum interval has passed
Salesforce will convert it into a Full sandbox
The refresh will succeed but data will not be updated

questions.explanation: B is correct. Partial Copy sandboxes have a minimum refresh interval of 5 days. Attempting to refresh before that window elapses results in an error or a queued refresh. A is wrong because the interval is enforced. C and D are fabricated behaviors.

questions.scenario: AW Computing follows a standard application lifecycle: developers build in isolated sandboxes, changes are integrated into a shared environment for testing, then promoted to a staging environment for UAT, and finally released to production.
questions.question: Which sandbox strategy correctly maps to this lifecycle?

options.text: Developer sandbox for dev, Partial Copy for integration, Full for UAT, then production
Developer sandbox for dev, Developer Pro for integration, Partial Copy for UAT, Full for staging, then production
Full sandbox for dev, Developer Pro for integration, Partial Copy for UAT, then production
Partial Copy for dev, Full for integration and UAT, then production

questions.explanation: B correctly aligns the environments with lifecycle stages: individual developers use Developer sandboxes, integration testing uses a shared Developer Pro sandbox for larger metadata volumes, UAT with sample data uses Partial Copy, and staging/regression rehearsal uses Full. A skips staging. C wastes a Full sandbox on development. D uses expensive Full sandboxes for early lifecycle stages.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty is adopting a modern source-driven development model with Git version control, Salesforce CLI, and automated CI/CD pipelines.
questions.question: Which Salesforce tool is the recommended modern deployment solution for declarative teams that want a UI-based release pipeline without writing scripts?

options.text: Change Sets
DevOps Center
Ant Migration Tool
Workbench

questions.explanation: B (DevOps Center) is correct. It is Salesforce's modern, UI-based release management tool that integrates with Git and enables source-driven development for admins and developers without CLI scripting. A (Change Sets) is a legacy tool with many limitations. C (Ant Migration Tool) is a legacy CLI-based Metadata API tool. D (Workbench) is a data/metadata utility, not a release pipeline.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers is modernizing its release process and evaluating source-driven development.
questions.question: Which two are benefits of source-driven development using Git and unlocked packages? (Choose 2)

options.text: Version control history for all metadata changes
Automatic deletion of production data on deployment
Ability to modularize metadata into upgradable packages
Elimination of the need for any sandbox testing

questions.explanation: A and C are correct benefits: version control tracks every change and enables collaboration, and unlocked packages allow modular, upgradable deployment units that can be versioned and released independently. B is false—deployments never touch production data automatically. D is false—sandboxes remain essential for testing before production.
questions.reference: Trailhead: Application Lifecycle and Development Models

questions.scenario: An AW Computing admin wants to deploy a new custom object and related fields from a Developer sandbox to production using change sets.
questions.question: What must be configured before the change set can be sent?

options.text: A namespace prefix in the target org
An authorized deployment connection between the two orgs
A managed package license
A remote site setting in production

questions.explanation: B is correct. Change sets require a deployment connection between related orgs (a production org and its sandboxes, or between sandboxes of the same production). The target org must authorize inbound change sets from the source. A is only needed for managed packages. C is unrelated. D is for callouts, not deployments.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to send a change set from one production org (Org A) to a completely unrelated production org (Org B) belonging to a partner company.
questions.question: What will happen?

options.text: The change set will deploy successfully once both admins approve it
Change sets cannot be used because the orgs are unrelated
Only custom objects will deploy; other metadata will fail
Salesforce will automatically create a deployment connection

questions.explanation: B is correct. Change sets only work between related orgs—the production org and its sandboxes, or between sandboxes that share the same production. Two unrelated production orgs must use another tool such as Metadata API, unmanaged/managed packages, or the CLI. A, C, and D are incorrect because no deployment connection can be established between unrelated orgs.

questions.scenario: NTO's admin needs to remove an obsolete custom field and a deprecated Apex class from production. The admin plans to use a change set.
questions.question: What is the correct outcome?

options.text: The change set will delete both components upon deployment
Change sets cannot delete metadata; the admin must use destructiveChanges.xml via Metadata API
Deleting an Apex class requires a managed package
The change set will delete the field but leave the Apex class

questions.explanation: B is correct. Change sets can only add or update metadata—they cannot delete components. To delete metadata in a deployment, use a destructiveChanges.xml manifest with the Metadata API (via Ant Migration Tool, SF CLI, or Workbench). A, C, and D misrepresent change set capabilities.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Deleting Components from an Organization

questions.scenario: A DreamHouse Realty admin adds a new custom field to the Property object in a change set but forgets to add the page layout that references it.
questions.question: What is the best practice regarding change set ordering and component dependencies?

options.text: Fields must be uploaded and deployed in a change set before layouts that reference them, or included in the same change set
Layouts should be deployed first, then fields
Change sets automatically resolve all dependencies
Fields and layouts must be in separate change sets deployed weeks apart

questions.explanation: A is correct. When deploying dependent metadata, prerequisites must exist in the target org first. Fields must exist before layouts that reference them—either include both in one change set or deploy the field first. The 'View/Add Dependencies' button in change sets helps identify related components. B reverses the order. C is false—admins must manage dependencies. D is unnecessary.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Change Set Best Practices

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar's release manager uploads a change set containing several Apex classes and triggers. Before deploying to production, the manager wants to confirm the deployment will succeed without actually applying the changes.
questions.question: Which action should the manager take?

options.text: Deploy the change set and immediately quick-deploy the rollback
Click 'Validate' on the inbound change set to run tests without committing changes
Manually recreate the components in production
Wait 24 hours and Salesforce will automatically pre-validate

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Validate option runs a deployment simulation—including required Apex tests—without committing changes. If validation succeeds within the last 10 days, it can be quick-deployed later without rerunning tests. A is not a real feature. C defeats the purpose. D is fabricated behavior.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks is preparing a change set that includes new profile settings for the Sales Rep profile.
questions.question: Which two statements about deploying profile settings in change sets are true? (Choose 2)

options.text: Change sets deploy only the profile settings for components included in the change set, not the entire profile
Change sets always overwrite the entire target profile with the source profile
Selecting 'Profile Settings for Included Components' brings across just the relevant permissions
Profile settings cannot be deployed through change sets under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A and C are correct. When you add profiles to a change set with the 'Profile Settings for Included Components' option, only the permissions and settings for the components in that change set are deployed—not the full profile. This protects target-org customizations. B is wrong because change sets do not overwrite the whole profile. D is wrong because profile settings can be deployed.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Profile Settings in Change Sets

questions.scenario: An AW Computing admin uploaded an outbound change set from a Developer sandbox to production yesterday. Today the admin realizes one Apex class was missing.
questions.question: What is the correct action to add the missing class?

options.text: Modify the already-uploaded outbound change set and re-upload
Uploaded (outbound) change sets are locked; clone it, add the class, and upload the new change set
Ask Salesforce Support to unlock the change set
Delete the inbound change set in production and re-upload

questions.explanation: B is correct. Once an outbound change set is uploaded, it is locked and cannot be modified. The standard practice is to clone the change set, add the missing components, and upload the new version. A is not possible. C is not a supported request. D does not help because the outbound side is locked.

questions.scenario: A Universal Containers admin wants to know which metadata components are supported in change sets.
questions.question: Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: All Salesforce metadata types are supported
Only Apex components are supported
Change sets support a specific list of metadata types; unsupported types must be deployed via Metadata API or packages
Only clicks-not-code components are supported

questions.explanation: C is correct. Change sets support a documented subset of metadata types. Unsupported types (e.g., some settings, certain new features on release) must be moved with the Metadata API, unmanaged packages, or manually recreated. A and D are false—many types are unsupported. B is false—many declarative components are supported.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Components Available in Change Sets

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks wants to distribute a set of custom objects and Apex code to another Salesforce org, with the receiving admin free to edit or modify the components after installation.
questions.question: Which package type should be used?

options.text: Unmanaged package
First-generation managed package
Second-generation managed package
Managed - Extension package

questions.explanation: A is correct. Unmanaged packages are open to editing after installation, do not support upgrades, and are typically used for one-time distributions such as templates, sample code, or migrations. B, C, and D are managed packages—they lock down components (IP protection) and support versioned upgrades but the subscriber cannot modify core components.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Managed vs Unmanaged Packages

questions.scenario: An ISV, DreamHouse Realty Apps, publishes a paid property-management app on the AppExchange. The ISV wants to protect its intellectual property and push seamless upgrades to customers.
questions.question: Which package type is required?

options.text: Unmanaged package
Managed package
Unlocked package
Extension package

questions.explanation: B (Managed package) is correct. Managed packages are required for AppExchange listings, protect IP through a namespace, allow the ISV to push upgrades, and prevent subscribers from modifying core components. A is not upgradable and offers no IP protection. C (Unlocked) is designed for internal use, not ISV distribution. D (Extension) is a supplementary package that depends on a base managed package.

questions.scenario: NTO's platform team wants a modern, source-driven packaging model for internal application modules that can be versioned in Git, deployed to multiple orgs, and upgraded—without requiring a namespace or AppExchange distribution.
questions.question: Which packaging option best fits?

options.text: First-generation managed package
Second-generation unlocked package
Second-generation managed package
Unmanaged package

questions.explanation: B is correct. Unlocked packages (a form of 2GP) are designed for internal, source-driven development. They can be versioned in Git, deployed and upgraded across orgs, and do not require a namespace (though one is supported). A (1GP managed) is legacy and IP-protected. C (2GP managed) is for ISVs. D (unmanaged) cannot be upgraded.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar's admin is reviewing what subscribers can and cannot do after installing a managed package from the AppExchange.
questions.question: Which two statements are true about subscriber orgs with an installed managed package? (Choose 2)

options.text: Subscribers can add new custom fields to objects from the managed package
Subscribers can modify the Apex code inside the managed package
Subscribers can extend the package with their own components without modifying core managed components
Subscribers can delete managed components at will

questions.explanation: A and C are correct. Subscribers can add new fields to objects delivered by a managed package, and they can extend functionality with their own components (workflows, flows, LWCs, etc.) that reference the package. B is false—managed Apex is locked. D is false—managed components can only be removed by uninstalling the package.
questions.reference: Salesforce Help: Managed Package Behavior in Subscriber Orgs

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks published an unmanaged package for a template solution and now wants to release version 2.0 with additional objects and bug fixes. Existing customers should upgrade seamlessly.
questions.question: What is the correct outcome?

options.text: Customers will receive an in-place upgrade with all existing customizations preserved
Unmanaged packages do not support upgrades; a new install is required and may cause conflicts
Cloud Kicks can convert the unmanaged package to managed and push the upgrade
Salesforce will automatically merge the new version into the customer org

questions.explanation: B is correct. Unmanaged packages are one-time distributions and cannot be upgraded. Customers must install the new version separately, and any customizations they made can conflict. A is false. C is not automatic—you cannot convert an unmanaged package to managed in place; you must repackage with a namespace. D is fabricated.

questions.scenario: An AppExchange ISV wants prospects to try their app with sample data and preconfigured metadata before purchasing.
questions.question: Which Salesforce feature enables this?

options.text: Trialforce
Change Sets
Unmanaged Package
DevOps Center

questions.explanation: A (Trialforce) is correct. Trialforce enables ISVs to create and distribute trial orgs that include their managed package with sample data and configuration, so prospects can evaluate the app. B is a deployment tool between related orgs. C is a distribution mechanism without trial capability. D is a release management tool.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers' Center of Excellence wants to organize their custom code and metadata into reusable, versioned modules that different business units can install independently, with the ability to upgrade in place. They do NOT want to sell the packages externally.
questions.question: Which packaging strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: One large unmanaged package that gets replaced each release
Multiple 2GP unlocked packages, each versioned in Git
A single 1GP managed package with namespace
Deploy everything via change sets only

questions.explanation: B is correct. 2GP unlocked packages are purpose-built for internal, modular, source-driven, upgradable deployments. Each module can be versioned in Git and installed/upgraded independently. A cannot be upgraded. C is over-engineered for internal use (namespaces are largely irrelevant for internal packages and complicate development). D is not a modular or versioned approach.

questions.scenario: AW Computing's release plan: build in Developer sandbox, integrate in Developer Pro, UAT in Partial Copy, stage in Full, then production. The team wants a modern, UI-based deployment tool integrated with Git that supports both admins and developers.
questions.question: Which tool should they adopt for the release pipeline?

options.text: Change Sets
DevOps Center
Data Loader
Schema Builder

questions.explanation: B (DevOps Center) is correct. It is Salesforce's modern release management tool designed to replace change sets, integrating with Git and supporting a source-driven pipeline from work items to release branches. A (Change Sets) is legacy and lacks Git integration. C is for data, not metadata. D is for schema design.

questions.scenario: Cloud Kicks is deploying a large release to production. The release includes new flows, Apex classes, new custom fields, and updated profile settings.
questions.question: Which three post-deployment steps are typically required? (Choose 3)

options.text: Activate deployed flows if they arrived inactive
Refresh the production sandbox before go-live
Assign or verify permission sets for new features
Run post-deployment data scripts if metadata changes require data updates
Delete all sandboxes to save storage

questions.explanation: A, C, and D are all standard post-deployment tasks. Flows often deploy as inactive and must be activated. New objects/fields may require permission set assignments so users can see them. Data scripts (e.g., populating a new field for existing records) are commonly needed. B is nonsensical—production is not a sandbox. E is destructive and unnecessary.

questions.scenario: DreamHouse Realty needs to deploy a complex release that includes deletions of obsolete metadata, new metadata, and updates—all in one coordinated push.
questions.question: Which deployment approach best supports all three actions in one operation?

options.text: Change sets only
Salesforce CLI with a Metadata API deployment including destructiveChanges.xml
Manual configuration in production
Data Loader

questions.scenario: NTO is a regulated financial services firm. Any change deployed to production must be tested in an environment that mirrors production data and configuration exactly. Auditors require evidence of a full pre-production rehearsal.
questions.question: Which sandbox should be used for the final pre-production rehearsal?

options.text: Developer sandbox
Developer Pro sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
Full sandbox

questions.explanation: D (Full) is correct. Compliance-driven scenarios that require a production mirror—including all data—need a Full sandbox for the staging/pre-production rehearsal. A and B lack production data. C only has a sample of data and is not a full mirror—insufficient for regulated audit evidence.

questions.scenario: Universal Containers wants to deploy a small hotfix (one Apex class change) to production quickly. The change was tested yesterday in a Developer sandbox that is a related sandbox of production.
questions.question: What is the fastest safe approach?

options.text: Use a change set from the Developer sandbox to production, validate first, then quick-deploy
Edit the class directly in production
Create a managed package to distribute the hotfix
Refresh a Full sandbox first, then deploy

questions.explanation: A is correct. A change set from a related sandbox to production is a valid path. Running Validate first (which executes required tests) allows a quick-deploy afterward, minimizing downtime. B may be technically possible for Apex only in Developer/Developer Pro sandboxes—not production, where Apex cannot be edited directly. C is overkill for a single class. D wastes time and offers no benefit for a one-class fix.

questions.scenario: Ursa Major Solar's admin team is choosing between change sets and DevOps Center for their new release process.
questions.question: Which two are advantages of DevOps Center over change sets? (Choose 2)

options.text: Git-based source control with full change history
Ability to deploy between two completely unrelated production orgs without any prior configuration
Automated pull of changes from a sandbox into a work item, with pipeline promotion between environments
Automatic deletion of production users

questions.explanation: A and C are advantages. DevOps Center brings Git version control and a work-item + pipeline model where changes flow from a Dev environment through UAT to production, with visibility and rollback. B is false—DevOps Center also requires connected orgs and a source control integration; it does not magically link unrelated orgs. D is fabricated and irrelevant.
